## Overview

This reproducible report evaluates whether passenger sex, ticket class, and age were associated with Titanic survival. Four nested binary logistic regression models are compared using likelihood-ratio tests, AIC, and BIC. The preferred model is examined using diagnostics, interpreted using log-odds and odds ratios, and visualized using predicted survival probabilities.

## Part 1: Configure the project and examine the data

### 1.1. Required packages

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)
```

### 1.2. Load the data

```{r}
#| label: load-data

titanic <- titanic_train |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1
    ),
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived"
    ),
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == 1 ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == 2 ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == 3 ~ "Third Class"
    ),
    Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3)),
    Sex = factor(Sex, levels = c("female", "male"))
  ) |>
  select(
    Survived,
    Survived.Char,
    Sex,
    Sex.Binary,
    Pclass,
    Pclass.Char,
    Age
  )

n <- nrow(titanic)

stopifnot(n == 714)
```

The complete-case sample contains `r n` passengers. `Survived` is coded 0 (died) and 1 (survived); `Sex`, `Age`, and `Pclass` are predictors. Passenger class is used as an imperfect proxy for socioeconomic status.

### 1.3. Descriptive statistics and category counts

```{r}
#| label: descriptives

age_stats <- titanic |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Age),
    SD = sd(Age),
    Min = min(Age),
    Max = max(Age)
  )

age_stats |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Passenger Age") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = everything(),
    decimals = 2
  )

counts <- bind_rows(
  titanic |>
    count(Category = Survived.Char) |>
    mutate(Variable = "Survival"),

  titanic |>
    count(Category = as.character(Sex)) |>
    mutate(Variable = "Sex"),

  titanic |>
    count(Category = Pclass.Char) |>
    mutate(Variable = "Passenger class")
) |>
  select(
    Variable,
    Category,
    Count = n
  )

counts |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Variable") |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Cell Counts for Categorical Variables"
  )
```

Mean age was `r sprintf('%.2f', age_stats$Mean)` years (SD = `r sprintf('%.2f', age_stats$SD)`; range `r age_stats$Min`–`r age_stats$Max`). There were `r sum(titanic$Survived == 1)` survivors and `r sum(titanic$Survived == 0)` non-survivors.

There were `r sum(titanic$Sex == 'female')` females and `r sum(titanic$Sex == 'male')` males. Third class accounted for `r sum(titanic$Pclass == '3')` of the `r n` passengers, more than either other class.

The categorical groups were not equally represented, and a minority of passengers survived.

## Part 2: Specify competing binary logistic regression models

### 2.1. Substantive predictions

I predict that females had higher survival chances than males because historical emergency evacuation practices could prioritize women.

I also predict higher survival for first-class passengers because ticket class may have been related to access to lifeboats or evacuation routes.

Age may be associated with survival because children could have been prioritized, although a single linear age term may not fully capture child-versus-adult differences.

These are hypotheses about associations, not causal conclusions.

### 2.2. Four nested models

The models add predictors in the order **Sex, Pclass, Age**. All four models use the same 714 complete cases and the same binomial logit link.

```{r}
#| label: fit-models

mod0 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ 1,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
```

### 2.3. Inspect the fitted coefficients

```{r}
#| label: fitted-coefficients

model_terms <- bind_rows(
  tidy(
    mod0,
    effects = "fixed",
    component = "cond"
  ) |>
    mutate(Model = "mod0"),

  tidy(
    mod1,
    effects = "fixed",
    component = "cond"
  ) |>
    mutate(Model = "mod1"),

  tidy(
    mod2,
    effects = "fixed",
    component = "cond"
  ) |>
    mutate(Model = "mod2"),

  tidy(
    mod3,
    effects = "fixed",
    component = "cond"
  ) |>
    mutate(Model = "mod3")
) |>
  select(
    Model,
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    p.value
  )

model_terms |>
  mutate(
    p.value = ifelse(
      p.value < .001,
      "< .001",
      sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
    )
  ) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Model") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, std.error),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Coefficient",
    estimate = "Log-odds",
    std.error = "SE",
    p.value = "p-value"
  )
```

The null-model intercept is the log-odds of survival across all passengers.

In `mod1`, the intercept describes female passengers, the reference sex.

In `mod2`, it describes first-class female passengers.

In `mod3`, it describes first-class female passengers at age zero, which is mathematically valid but not a typical passenger age. Therefore, interpreting the intercept substantively requires caution.

Other coefficients are adjusted for the predictors included in their respective models.

## Part 3: Compare model performance

### 3.1. Nested likelihood-ratio tests

The models are nested and estimated on identical cases. The following comparison evaluates whether each successive model improves fit over the preceding model.

```{r}
#| label: nested-tests

nested_tests <- anova(
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3
)

nested_tests
```

### 3.2. Extract model-level performance using `glance()`

```{r}
#| label: glance-models

model_list <- list(
  mod0 = mod0,
  mod1 = mod1,
  mod2 = mod2,
  mod3 = mod3
)

model_stats <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(model_list), function(name) {

    model <- model_list[[name]]
    g <- broom.mixed::glance(model)

    data.frame(
      Model = name,
      AIC = g$AIC,
      BIC = g$BIC,
      logLik = as.numeric(logLik(model)),
      deviance = -2 * as.numeric(logLik(model)),
      Residual_df = df.residual(model)
    )
  })
)
```

### 3.3. Combined model-comparison table

```{r}
#| label: combined-model-table

nested_df <- data.frame(
  Model = rownames(nested_tests),
  Nested_df = nested_tests[["Chi Df"]],
  Nested_Chi2 = nested_tests[["Chisq"]],
  Nested_p = nested_tests[["Pr(>Chisq)"]]
)

comparison <- left_join(
  model_stats,
  nested_df,
  by = "Model"
)

comparison |>
  mutate(
    Nested_p = ifelse(
      is.na(Nested_p),
      "—",
      ifelse(
        Nested_p < .001,
        "< .001",
        sprintf("%.3f", Nested_p)
      )
    )
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Four Nested Logistic Regression Models"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested_Chi2
    ),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      Residual_df,
      Nested_df
    ),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    logLik = "logLik",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    Residual_df = "Residual df",
    Nested_df = "Nested df",
    Nested_Chi2 = "Nested Chi-square",
    Nested_p = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(
      Nested_df,
      Nested_Chi2
    ),
    missing_text = "—"
  )
```

### 3.4. Interpret model comparisons

The full model, `mod3`, had the lowest AIC (`r sprintf('%.2f', AIC(mod3))`) and BIC (`r sprintf('%.2f', BIC(mod3))`) of the four candidate models.

Adding sex to the null model produced the largest improvement in fit, χ²(1) = 213.82, *p* < .001.

Adding passenger class after sex also significantly improved fit, χ²(2) = 78.27, *p* < .001.

Finally, adding age after accounting for both sex and passenger class significantly improved fit, χ²(1) = 25.15, *p* < .001.

Although adding predictors increases model complexity, the improvements in likelihood were sufficiently large to outweigh the complexity penalties used by AIC and BIC.

Therefore, all three approaches support retaining `mod3` as the preferred model among those evaluated. The sequential improvements depend on the order in which predictors enter the models and should not be interpreted as definitive rankings of causal importance.

## Part 4: Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

### 4.1. DHARMa simulation-based residual diagnostics

Simulation-based residual diagnostics were used to examine residual uniformity, dispersion, outliers, and relationships between residuals and fitted predictions.

The plots are constructed using `ggplot2` to avoid overlapping statistical annotations. Formal DHARMa tests are reported separately.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-residuals

set.seed(123)

sim_res <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = mod3,
  n = 1000
)

diagnostic_data <- data.frame(
  scaled_residual = sim_res$scaledResiduals,
  fitted_probability = as.numeric(
    predict(mod3, type = "response")
  ),
  Age = titanic$Age
)

qq_data <- data.frame(
  Expected = ppoints(nrow(diagnostic_data)),
  Observed = sort(diagnostic_data$scaled_residual)
)
```

### 4.1.1. Residual uniformity QQ plot

```{r}
#| label: clean-qq
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  qq_data,
  aes(
    x = Expected,
    y = Observed
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 0.8,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    color = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "DHARMa Residual Uniformity",
    x = "Expected Quantile",
    y = "Observed Quantile"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 4.1.2. Residuals versus predicted probability

```{r}
#| label: clean-residuals-predictions
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  diagnostic_data,
  aes(
    x = fitted_probability,
    y = scaled_residual
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = .35,
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(.25, .5, .75),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey65"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "DHARMa Residuals Versus Predicted Survival",
    x = "Predicted Probability",
    y = "Scaled Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 4.1.3. Residuals versus age

```{r}
#| label: clean-residuals-age
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(
  diagnostic_data,
  aes(
    x = Age,
    y = scaled_residual
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = .30,
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "steelblue",
    linewidth = .8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "DHARMa Residuals Versus Age",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Scaled Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 4.1.4. Statistical tests

```{r}
#| label: dharma-tests

uniformity_test <- DHARMa::testUniformity(
  sim_res,
  plot = FALSE
)

dispersion_test <- DHARMa::testDispersion(
  sim_res,
  plot = FALSE
)

outlier_test <- DHARMa::testOutliers(
  sim_res,
  plot = FALSE
)

diag_table <- data.frame(
  Test = c(
    "Residual uniformity",
    "Dispersion",
    "Outliers"
  ),
  Statistic = c(
    unname(uniformity_test$statistic),
    unname(dispersion_test$statistic),
    unname(outlier_test$statistic)
  ),
  p_value = c(
    uniformity_test$p.value,
    dispersion_test$p.value,
    outlier_test$p.value
  )
)

diag_table |>
  mutate(
    p_value = ifelse(
      p_value < .001,
      "< .001",
      sprintf("%.3f", p_value)
    )
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "DHARMa Diagnostic Tests"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = Statistic,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    p_value = "p-value"
  )
```

The residual uniformity test (*p* = `r sprintf('%.3f', uniformity_test$p.value)`) and dispersion test (*p* = `r sprintf('%.3f', dispersion_test$p.value)`) did not indicate statistically significant departures from the expected residual behaviour.

The outlier test (*p* = `r sprintf('%.3f', outlier_test$p.value)`) approached the conventional .05 significance threshold, warranting some caution.

### 4.2. Collinearity

```{r}
#| label: collinearity

performance::check_collinearity(mod3)
```

Variance inflation factors (VIFs) were used to examine collinearity among the predictors. The observed VIFs ranged from 1.07 to 1.42, indicating low collinearity and suggesting that strong relationships among predictors were unlikely to substantially inflate the coefficient standard errors.

### 4.3. Complete separation and event counts

```{r}
#| label: separation-event-checks

# Observed survival outcomes within sex and class
xtabs(
  ~ Sex + Pclass + Survived,
  data = titanic
)

# Range of fitted probabilities
range(
  as.numeric(
    predict(mod3, type = "response")
  )
)

# Check for finite coefficients
all(is.finite(fixef(mod3)$cond))

# Number of survival events per slope coefficient
number_of_events <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)

number_of_slopes <- length(
  fixef(mod3)$cond
) - 1

number_of_events / number_of_slopes
```

There were `r number_of_events` survival events for `r number_of_slopes` slope coefficients, corresponding to `r round(number_of_events / number_of_slopes, 1)` events per coefficient.

All sex-by-class combinations contained both survivors and non-survivors, and the fitted coefficients were finite. These findings do not indicate obvious separation among the categorical groups. However, they cannot conclusively rule out separation involving continuous age.

### 4.4. Linearity of age on the logit scale

The final model assumes that age has a linear relationship with the log-odds of survival.

To assess this assumption, a linear age model was compared with a more flexible natural-spline specification.

```{r}
#| label: age-linearity

age_linear <- glm(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age,
  family = binomial(),
  data = titanic
)

age_spline <- glm(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + splines::ns(Age, df = 3),
  family = binomial(),
  data = titanic
)

linearity_comparison <- anova(
  age_linear,
  age_spline,
  test = "Chisq"
)

linearity_comparison
```

The spline model did not significantly improve fit over the linear specification, χ²(2) = 5.14, *p* = .077.

Therefore, there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the more flexible age specification provided a substantial improvement in fit, although this result does not establish that the linearity assumption is perfectly satisfied.

### 4.5. Potentially influential cases

Cook's distance was calculated using an equivalent binomial `glm()` model to identify observations potentially exerting disproportionate influence on coefficient estimates.

```{r}
#| label: influence

cook_values <- cooks.distance(age_linear)

cook_cutoff <- 4 / nrow(titanic)

influence_summary <- data.frame(
  Threshold = cook_cutoff,
  Cases_above_threshold = sum(
    cook_values > cook_cutoff,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ),
  Maximum_Cooks_D = max(
    cook_values,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
)

influence_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      Threshold,
      Maximum_Cooks_D
    ),
    decimals = 4
  )
```

The analysis identified 47 observations exceeding the heuristic Cook's distance threshold of 4/n (0.0056). However, the maximum Cook's distance was 0.029.

Exceeding this screening threshold does not automatically indicate that observations should be removed. Rather, these cases warrant consideration when assessing the robustness of model estimates.

### 4.6. Diagnostic interpretation

Simulation-based residual diagnostics did not identify statistically significant departures from the fitted model's assumptions. The uniformity test (*p* = .512) and dispersion test (*p* = .814) were nonsignificant. The outlier test approached, but did not reach, the conventional significance threshold (*p* = .057).

Collinearity was low, with variance inflation factors ranging from 1.07 to 1.42. The comparison between linear and spline specifications for age was also nonsignificant, χ²(2) = 5.14, *p* = .077, providing insufficient evidence that a more flexible age specification substantially improved fit.

The influence analysis identified 47 observations exceeding the heuristic Cook's distance threshold of 4/n, although the maximum Cook's distance was relatively small (0.029). These observations may warrant further examination, but exceeding this threshold does not automatically indicate that they should be excluded.

Overall, the diagnostics did not reveal strong evidence of model inadequacy, although the borderline outlier result, potentially influential observations, and assumptions about the functional form of age should be acknowledged when interpreting the findings.

## Part 5: Select and report the preferred model

### 5.1. Model selection

The preferred model was `mod3`, containing sex, passenger class, and age.

It had the lowest AIC (657.28) and BIC (680.14), and each successive addition of predictors significantly improved model fit.

The final model was retained because it provided the best balance of model fit and complexity among the four candidate specifications.

Its interpretation remains conditional on the diagnostic findings described in Part 4.

### 5.2. Coefficient table using `broom.mixed::tidy()`

```{r}
#| label: tidy-coefficients

coef_results <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  mod3,
  effects = "fixed",
  component = "cond",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = .95
) |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    OR_lower = exp(conf.low),
    OR_upper = exp(conf.high),

    p_display = ifelse(
      p.value < .001,
      "< .001",
      sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
    ),

    Predictor = recode(
      term,
      "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
      "Sexmale" = "Male (vs female)",
      "Pclass2" = "Second class (vs first)",
      "Pclass3" = "Third class (vs first)",
      "Age" = "Age (one year)"
    )
  )

coef_results |>
  select(
    Predictor,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p_display
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Preferred Model Coefficients (Log-odds Scale)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      estimate,
      std.error,
      conf.low,
      conf.high
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI Lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI Upper",
    p_display = "p-value"
  )

coef_results |>
  select(
    Predictor,
    OR,
    OR_lower,
    OR_upper,
    p_display
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Preferred Model Odds Ratios"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      OR,
      OR_lower,
      OR_upper
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    OR = "Odds Ratio",
    OR_lower = "95% CI Lower",
    OR_upper = "95% CI Upper",
    p_display = "p-value"
  )
```

### 5.3. Interpret log-odds and odds ratios

```{r}
#| label: interpretation-helper

term_value <- function(term_name, variable) {
  coef_results |>
    filter(term == term_name) |>
    pull({{ variable }})
}
```

**Sex**

The coefficient for males was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Sexmale', estimate))` log-odds units, compared with females of the same age and passenger class.

The corresponding odds ratio was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Sexmale', OR))` (95% CI `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Sexmale', OR_lower))`–`r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Sexmale', OR_upper))`).

Thus, male passengers had approximately `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * (1 - term_value('Sexmale', OR)))`% lower odds of surviving, conditional on age and passenger class.

**Passenger class**

Relative to first class, the second-class coefficient was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass2', estimate))` log-odds units (OR = `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass2', OR))`, 95% CI `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass2', OR_lower))`–`r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass2', OR_upper))`).

The third-class coefficient was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass3', estimate))` (OR = `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass3', OR))`, 95% CI `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass3', OR_lower))`–`r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass3', OR_upper))`).

Both comparisons hold age and sex constant. Second- and third-class passengers had lower estimated odds of survival than first-class passengers.

**Age**

Each additional year of age was associated with a `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Age', estimate))` change in log-odds of survival, holding sex and class constant.

The odds ratio per year was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Age', OR))` (95% CI `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Age', OR_lower))`–`r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Age', OR_upper))`), corresponding to approximately `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * (1 - term_value('Age', OR)))`% lower odds of survival per additional year under the assumed linear age effect.

### 5.4. Preferred-model overall performance

```{r}
#| label: final-performance

model_stats |>
  filter(Model == "mod3") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Overall Performance: Preferred Model"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance
    ),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Residual_df = "Residual df"
  )
```

### 5.5. Overall result

The nested model comparisons demonstrated that sex, passenger class, and age were associated with survival outcomes.

In the adjusted final model, the male-versus-female odds ratio was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Sexmale', OR))`, the second-versus-first-class odds ratio was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass2', OR))`, the third-versus-first-class odds ratio was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Pclass3', OR))`, and the per-year age odds ratio was `r sprintf('%.3f', term_value('Age', OR))`.

These associations are observational and do not establish that any individual predictor caused survival outcomes.

### 5.6. Visualize predicted probabilities using `ggeffects::ggpredict()`

Passenger class is shown at the sample mean age with separate series for sex.

These are model-adjusted predicted probabilities rather than raw group survival rates.

```{r}
#| label: ggeffects-prediction

predicted <- ggeffects::ggpredict(
  mod3,
  terms = c(
    "Pclass",
    "Sex",
    paste0(
      "Age [",
      round(mean(titanic$Age), 5),
      "]"
    )
  )
)

predicted_df <- as.data.frame(predicted) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass = factor(
      as.character(x),
      levels = c("1", "2", "3"),
      labels = c(
        "First Class",
        "Second Class",
        "Third Class"
      )
    ),
    Sex = as.character(group)
  )

predicted_df |>
  select(
    Pclass,
    Sex,
    predicted,
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Predicted Survival by Ticket Class and Sex"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      predicted,
      conf.low,
      conf.high
    ),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: ggeffects-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  predicted_df,
  aes(
    x = Pclass,
    y = predicted,
    color = Sex,
    group = Sex
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    position = position_dodge(width = .12)
  ) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = .8,
    position = position_dodge(width = .12)
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = conf.low,
      ymax = conf.high
    ),
    width = .12,
    position = position_dodge(width = .12)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Predicted Probability of Titanic Survival",
    subtitle = "Age held at sample mean; error bars show 95% confidence intervals",
    x = "Passenger Class",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Survival",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

At the mean passenger age of 29.70 years, predicted survival was highest among first-class female passengers (93.6%) and lowest among third-class male passengers (8.1%).

Within each passenger class, females had higher predicted probabilities of survival than males. Predicted survival also decreased from first to third class for both sexes.

These findings are consistent with the final model's odds ratios, which indicate substantial associations between survival, sex, and passenger class after adjusting for age.

## Part 6: Discussion and limitations

The findings indicate that passenger sex, ticket class, and age were associated with survival on the Titanic.

Sex produced the largest improvement in the sequential model comparisons, χ²(1) = 213.82, *p* < .001. Passenger class provided a further substantial improvement after controlling for sex, χ²(2) = 78.27, *p* < .001. Age also improved fit after both predictors were included, χ²(1) = 25.15, *p* < .001.

These sequential improvements suggest that sex and passenger class were particularly informative for predicting survival. However, the relative improvements depend on the order of model entry and should not be treated as direct measures of causal importance.

The final model indicates markedly lower odds of survival for males and passengers in lower ticket classes. Increasing age was also associated with lower odds of survival after adjusting for sex and class.

Several limitations qualify these findings. Ticket class is an imperfect proxy for socioeconomic position, and the observational dataset cannot establish causal relationships.

Unmeasured factors, including physical location aboard the ship, travel companions, and access to evacuation routes, could partly explain the observed associations.

The complete-case analysis excluded passengers with missing age values, potentially introducing selection bias if missingness was related to passenger characteristics or survival.

Finally, the model assumes linear age effects on the logit scale and does not include interactions. These assumptions may overlook differences between children and adults or variations in sex-related survival patterns across passenger classes.

Overall, the analysis demonstrates that logistic regression can quantify associations between multiple predictors and a binary outcome while allowing competing model specifications to be evaluated using statistical evidence.
